title: Ancient Egypt and the Edwin Smith papyrus
text:
CHAPTER 1. EARLIEST IDEAS ABOUT THE BRAIN
SECTION 1.1. ANCIENT EGYPT AND THE EDWIN SMITH PAPYRUS

Why start with a papyrus?

If you study mechatronics, you are used to systems that have sensors, controllers, and actuators. You know that when a sensor cable is cut, the controller loses information, and when a motor cable is cut, the controller loses its ability to act. It seems obvious to us that the brain is the controller of the body. But that idea was not obvious to most people for most of human history. Many ancient cultures gave the heart, not the brain, the central role in thought, emotion, and memory. The story of neuroscience is in large part the story of how humans slowly collected evidence that the brain is the organ of the mind, and then how they learned what the brain is made of and how it computes.

The oldest substantial written document that describes the brain in a medical way is an Egyptian text known today as the Edwin Smith papyrus. It is a good starting point because it shows something that will repeat throughout this book: careful observation of what happens when a system is damaged can reveal how the system works. In engineering terms, the Egyptian physicians were doing fault analysis on the human body.

The document and its name

The papyrus is named after Edwin Smith, an American dealer and collector of antiquities who bought it in Egypt in the nineteenth century (the purchase is usually dated to 1862, in Luxor). It is not named after its author, who is unknown. After Smith's death the papyrus was given to the New-York Historical Society, and it is now held by the New York Academy of Medicine. The first full translation into English, with a long commentary, was published by the Egyptologist James Henry Breasted in 1930.

The papyrus is written in hieratic, a cursive script used by Egyptian scribes, and it is generally dated to around the seventeenth or sixteenth century BCE, during the late Second Intermediate Period or early New Kingdom. Many scholars believe, from features of the language and from explanatory glosses added to the text, that it is a copy of an older original, possibly going back several centuries earlier to the Old Kingdom. Because exact dates for such documents are uncertain, it is safest to say that the text we have is more than 3,500 years old and that its content may be older still.

What the papyrus contains

The papyrus is essentially a surgical textbook on trauma. It presents 48 cases, arranged roughly from the top of the body downward: head first, then the face, the neck, the shoulders, and the chest and upper spine. The text breaks off partway through, so we do not know how far down the body the original went.

Each case follows a structured format that will look familiar to anyone who has read an engineering procedure or a modern medical case report:

1. A title naming the injury.
2. An examination: what the physician should look at, palpate, or ask the patient to do.
3. A diagnosis.
4. A verdict, one of three types: an ailment "which I will treat", an ailment "with which I will contend", or an ailment "not to be treated". In other words, a prognosis of good, uncertain, or hopeless.
5. A treatment, where one is given.
6. In many cases, glosses that explain obscure terms in the older text.

This structure is important. It shows a rational, empirical approach. Most of the treatments are practical: binding wounds, using stitches or adhesive strips, applying fresh meat to the wound on the first day, honey, grease, and lint, and splints. Magic is not absent from Egyptian medicine as a whole, and there is an incantation on the back of the papyrus, but the 48 cases themselves are strikingly practical.

The brain in the papyrus

The papyrus contains what is widely considered the earliest known written description of the brain. The Egyptian word that Breasted and later translators render as "brain" appears in several of the head injury cases. The text compares the folded surface exposed in a skull fracture to the corrugations or ripples that form on molten metal or slag in a crucible. This is a vivid image, and to a modern reader it is clearly a description of the gyri, the folds of the cerebral cortex.

The papyrus also mentions the membranes covering the brain (what we call the meninges) and fluid beneath them, which many readers interpret as cerebrospinal fluid. And it describes the physician placing his fingers on a wound and feeling something throb or flutter beneath them, which is consistent with feeling the pulsation of the brain under a skull defect.

The most remarkable observations, for a neuroscientist, are the ones that link an injury in one place to a functional problem somewhere else. Several cases in the papyrus describe consequences of head injuries that we would today call neurological signs. Translators have read parts of the text as describing, for example:

- A patient with a head wound who cannot speak, or who is speechless for a period.
- A patient whose eye is turned or whose gaze is affected on one side.
- A patient who walks shuffling, or drags a foot, after a head injury.
- Injuries to the neck vertebrae that are followed by loss of movement and sensation in the arms and legs, along with other effects. In one well known case, a dislocated vertebra of the neck leads to the patient being unaware of his arms and legs. The papyrus classifies this as an ailment not to be treated.

How exactly to read each phrase is a matter for Egyptologists, and you will find small differences between translations. But the general picture is clear and widely accepted: the Egyptian author noticed that injuries to the head and spine could produce effects on speech, movement, and sensation in distant parts of the body. That is the basic observation from which all of clinical neurology grows.

A note of caution about interpretation

It is tempting to say that the ancient Egyptians "knew" the brain controls the body. That would be an overstatement. The papyrus records correlations between injuries and symptoms, carefully and without theory. It does not present a general doctrine that the brain is the seat of the mind. In wider Egyptian thought, the heart (the "ib") was regarded as the center of thought, feeling, and moral character. During mummification the heart was usually left in the body because it was needed in the afterlife, where it would be weighed against the feather of Maat. The brain, by contrast, was generally removed, often through the nose, and discarded; the Greek historian Herodotus describes the removal of the brain with an iron hook, though practice varied over time and not every mummy shows the same method.

So we have an interesting contrast. The clinical observations in the Edwin Smith papyrus point toward the brain and spinal cord as crucial for movement and sensation, while the broader culture placed mind and personality in the heart. This kind of gap between data and theory is not unique to the ancient world. In science and engineering, accurate observations often appear long before anyone has a framework that explains them.

Other Egyptian medical papyri

The Edwin Smith papyrus is not the only Egyptian medical text. The Ebers papyrus, of roughly similar date, is longer and covers internal medicine, remedies, and a theory of vessels (called "metu") that carry air, blood, mucus, and other substances through the body, with the heart as a central hub. The metu concept mixes what we would now separate into blood vessels, tendons, and possibly nerves. It is an early example of a "network" theory of the body, but the network is centered on the heart. Other papyri, such as the Kahun gynecological papyrus, deal with specialized topics. Compared with these, the Edwin Smith papyrus stands out for its focus on trauma and its relatively systematic, examination-based approach.

Who wrote it?

Because the author is unknown, people have sometimes linked the original text to Imhotep, the famous architect and official of the Third Dynasty who was later deified as a god of medicine. Breasted himself raised this possibility. However, there is no direct evidence that Imhotep wrote it, and most modern scholars treat the attribution as speculation. This is a good example of the accuracy rule for this book: when a historical claim is attractive but uncertain, we will say so.

What a mechatronics student can take from this

Think of the 48 cases as a dataset. Each case is a record of the form: (location and type of damage, observed signs, prognosis). The author was building, informally, a mapping from inputs (injuries) to outputs (symptoms and outcomes). Modern neurology and neuropsychology still do this. When a stroke damages a particular region and a patient loses a particular ability, we learn something about what that region contributes. This "lesion method" will appear again and again: in Broca's patient with language loss, in the patient H.M. with memory loss, and in animal experiments where a region is removed or silenced.

There are well known pitfalls with lesion data, and they are worth stating early because they apply equally to engineered systems:

1. Damage is rarely clean. A real injury affects several regions and the connections between them (the "wires"), not just one component.
2. A system may compensate. After damage, other parts of the brain may take over some functions, which can hide the original role of the damaged part.
3. Removing a part shows what the whole system cannot do without it, not exactly what the part does. If you cut the power cable to a robot arm, the arm stops moving, but that does not mean the power cable computes movement.

Neuroscience has spent centuries learning to reason carefully about this last point.

Bridge to AI: ablation studies

Modern machine learning uses a direct descendant of the lesion method, the ablation study. When researchers build a deep network, they often remove a component, such as a layer, an attention head, or a particular input feature, and measure how performance changes. In interpretability research, people also "knock out" individual neurons or directions inside a trained network to see which behaviors depend on them. The same cautions apply. Networks, like brains, have redundancy, so ablating one unit may show little effect even if the unit is used. And a large effect does not always mean the component "contains" the function; it might just be a necessary relay. When you read an AI paper with an ablation table, you are looking at the intellectual descendant of the Edwin Smith papyrus: a structured record of what breaks when a part is damaged.

There is a second connection. The papyrus organizes knowledge as cases with structured fields, and it gives explicit decision rules (treat, contend, do not treat). This is close to how early expert systems in AI were built: collections of if-then rules derived from human experts. Those systems were brittle because the world contains more cases than any rulebook. The brain, as we will see, solves this problem by learning from data, and so does modern machine learning.

Summary

- The Edwin Smith papyrus is an Egyptian surgical text, probably copied around the seventeenth or sixteenth century BCE from older material.
- It describes 48 trauma cases in a structured format of examination, diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment.
- It contains the earliest known written description of the brain, including a comparison of its surface folds to ripples in molten metal, and mentions of the meninges and fluid.
- It links head and spinal injuries to distant effects on speech, movement, and sensation, which is the root idea of clinical neurology.
- Egyptian culture nevertheless placed the mind in the heart, showing that observations and theory do not always agree.
- The lesion method that the papyrus implicitly uses survives today in neurology and in ablation studies in machine learning.
